title: Connecting occupational health and AI safety
description: Understand AI safety, its risks and how occupational health can contribute to the design, evaluation and deployment of safer AI.
keywords: Connecting occupational health and AI safety. AI safety aims to prevent the harm that artificial intelligence systems can cause to people and society. A team gets a tool that proposes a shift schedule. Who can spot overlapping shifts, correct the proposal and tell the colleagues affected? Occupational health teams can help answer those questions during design and again when the tool is in use. By Dr Charles Broutin , occupational physician · 16 November 2026 What occupational health can contribute. Safety depends on models and on their interactions with people and organisations. The sociotechnical approach proposed by Weidinger and colleagues connects these levels of evaluation. We propose bringing real work more fully into this approach through three contributions. Protect workers. Identify how AI changes workload, autonomy, skills and working relationships. Involving the people affected helps compare promised gains with actual constraints and develop preventive measures before difficulties become established. Report problems to the people who can fix them. Document verification time, errors and situations in which decisions become difficult to challenge. These observations can inform interface design, limits on use and resources for oversight, and be discussed with project leaders and developers. Examine safety work. People who develop, test and evaluate AI need to be able to check results, report problems and challenge decisions. Their deadlines, resources and working conditions are a research direction for understanding the quality of safety checks. From observation to a decision. An agent prepares case files, but employees no longer have time to verify its proposals. Measuring this workload could lead to narrowing the tool’s scope, making sources visible, allocating time for checks or suspending the pilot. Evidence from practice must be able to change the system and its deployment. Three families of risks. The International AI Safety Report 2026 groups general-purpose AI risks into three overlapping categories. The workplace examples below illustrate this framework. Malicious use Using AI to deceive or cause harm. A fake voice message from a company director asks an employee to transfer money. Malfunctions Errors and dangerous behaviours, including loss-of-control scenarios. An agent changes case files without sufficient verification. Systemic risks The effects of widespread AI adoption on the economy and society. Task substitution may weaken skills and bargaining power. The strength of evidence differs across risks. The economic risk of AI is not measured only in jobs lost. It lies in the place human work keeps in the creation of value. A gradual shift. Assist, recommend, decide by default, act autonomously: one task, one occupation and one decision at a time. Three possible consequences. Less bargaining power, the loss of the first rungs of careers, and a concentration of economic power. Signals visible early. Posts left unfilled, fewer junior hires, raised targets, more checking and correction work. A scenario, not a finding. It examines a possible systemic risk, not a demonstrated consequence of today’s AI. STARTING POINT The economic risk of artificial intelligence is not just a question: how many jobs will disappear? The change could be much more gradual. As models become capable of performing more intellectual tasks, using software, making decisions and acting autonomously, companies can gradually replace some human labour with another resource: capital, computation and AI models . The hypothesis developed in The Intelligence Curse is simple: if intelligence becomes a resource that can be purchased, copied and deployed almost at will, capital gradually becomes a substitute for labour. Organisations with sufficient resources can then directly purchase the capabilities they need instead of recruiting, training and retaining people. This shift does not require AI to suddenly replace all workers. It can happen one task, one job, and one decision at a time. 01 From copilot to economic infrastructure At first, AI is introduced as a productivity tool. It writes a document, analyses data, helps with programming, prepares a presentation or proposes a decision. By Dr Charles Broutin , occupational physician · Updated on 27 November 2026 Read the full chapter → Guide contents → The essentials A notion still in dispute. Direct answer Artificial general intelligence, or AGI, is a goal stated by several laboratories. There is neither a shared definition nor a test that would establish its arrival. A model can pass a knowledge exam and fail to organise a project over several days. Different definitions give those results different weight. Guide, chapter 09 01 / Approaches Three ways of defining it. Each sheds light on what is at stake for work. By work Outperforming humans at most jobs. OpenAI’s charter (2018) aims at “highly autonomous systems” that outperform humans at most economically valuable work. The definition is explicitly economic: it is measured by the substitution of human work. OpenAI Charter, 2018 ↗ By levels A progression rather than a threshold. Google DeepMind crosses the level of performance, from “emerging” to “superhuman”, with the breadth of tasks covered. The degree of autonomy left to the system is treated separately: it is a deployment choice, not only a capability. By Dr Charles Broutin , occupational physician · Updated on 27 November 2026 Read the full chapter → Guide contents → The essentials A prediction machine. Direct answer A large language model, or LLM, is a neural network trained to predict what comes next in a text. It does not look up a ready-made answer in a database: it composes one, unit by unit. If the notes mention a meeting on Thursday without giving a time, the model may supply a plausible time. Check the draft against the notes before sending it. These small units are taken from the prompt and the documents supplied: words, pieces of words or signs. Represent: tokens become numbers. These vectors encode the regularities learned during training. Relate: attention weighs the context. The Transformer examines the links between tokens to determine which matter most at that moment. Vaswani et al., 2017 ↗ Predict: the next token is chosen. The model computes a probability distribution. Generation settings influence the choice and how much it varies. Repeat: the answer is built step by step. The chosen token joins the context, and so on until the last one. Illustrative example After “The employee describes persistent pain in the…”, the model assigns a probability to each possible continuation: “back”, “wrist”, “knee”. It chooses what is probable in that context, not what is true for that employee. In the guide, the probabilities in this example are fictitious. 02 / How it is built Five training stages, and the flaw each can leave behind. An LLM’s capabilities are not programmed rule by rule.
